purpose: V14.3.1 is level 1 and FAIL: logout ends the session but does not clear what the session left behind. The route is otherwise careful - CSRF, upstream revoke, cookies cleared, no-store - which is why the gap was worth stating precisely. No response anywhere in the web application sent Clear-Site-Data, and assistant conversations, per-deal document lists and checklists, and the support profile all survived logout. This closes it on both sides and moves the requirement to PASS.
requiredInvariants: V14.3.3 is NOT touched and stays FAIL. That the support profile, assistant conversations and per-deal document lists are written to browser storage at all is a different requirement from clearing them at logout, and closing the second does not close the first.

V14.3.2 is NOT claimed either. The Clear-Site-Data value includes "cache" precisely because 27 route handlers still set no Cache-Control, but requesting a cache clear at logout is not the same as those handlers setting no-store, which is what V14.3.2 asks for.

"cookies" is deliberately NOT in the Clear-Site-Data value. A browser would clear cookies across the whole registrable domain, and this platform runs a separate control host whose session this logout must not touch. Cookie clearing stays with clearAuthenticatedSession, which clears exactly its own.
The CSRF-rejected path keeps no Clear-Site-Data header. A request that failed the check is not a logout, and a test asserts that direction so the header cannot be sprayed onto every response.
No production, REG.RU, DNS, database or credential mutation. No schema change, no migration, no dependency, no lockfile change. New mandatory cost: 0 RUB.
acceptance: The gap was measured before it was closed: zero occurrences of Clear-Site-Data anywhere in apps/web, and 99 tracked files touching localStorage, sessionStorage, indexedDB or caches. The persisted content was read rather than assumed - Gekta conversation history and project lists, DocumentsDropzone per-deal document lists and checklists under dynamic per-deal keys, the ChatSupportWidget support profile, command palette history and the header note.

Two mechanisms, and the second exists because the first has a boundary. Server: every response through the shared response() helper carries Clear-Site-Data "cache", "storage". Client: clearClientSessionState() clears both web storages synchronously and is called from the finally block of all four logout callers, so it runs when the request never reached the server - the exact gap the previous decision note named as missing.

The client path clears everything rather than a curated list of sensitive keys. A hand-maintained list means any new component that starts writing to storage silently falls outside it; deny-by-default is cheaper and safer. The cost is stated rather than hidden: interface theme and density reset to default at logout, which on a shared or borrowed device is closer to correct than to a loss.

The cleanup is synchronous on purpose, because logout navigates immediately afterwards and asynchronous work could be cut off. caches and service worker registrations are deliberately left to Clear-Site-Data in production and to V7CacheGuard on the next load - and unregistering service workers is not a new behaviour here, V7CacheGuard already does exactly that on a version change.

Seven cases. Four on the route, including the negative direction (a CSRF-rejected logout carries no header) and the placement assertion (the header lives in the shared response() helper, not on one path). Two on the helper, including a localStorage that throws on access, which is what a private window or disabled site data does - the logout must not fail and sessionStorage must still be cleared. One completeness test that enumerates logout callers by searching tracked sources rather than listing them by hand, so a fifth caller added later without the cleanup fails there rather than at review.

Four mutations against the tests, each caught by exactly the intended case: removing the header fails 3 of 7; adding "cookies" fails the case that forbids it; removing the cleanup from one caller fails the completeness test; making the helper a no-op fails 2.

The PASS is machine-revocable, and that was run rather than asserted. Three mutations were applied to the tree and the matrix rebuilt each time: removing the header, removing the cleanup from one of four callers, and making the helper a no-op. All three drove V14.3.1 from PASS to NOT_ASSESSED and the totals from 127/92 back to 126/92 with NOT_ASSESSED 38 -> 39. The decision carries three PRESENT_ALL_AT_PATH conditions, which require every named path to carry every named pattern.

web tsc --noEmit exit 0. node --test scripts/security/*.test.mjs 117/117. verify-decision-evidence exit 0 - it caught the new helper first as a cited file that was not yet tracked by git, which is the gate doing its job. verify-web-unit-coverage exit 0 with the new spec in the executed list. Cryptographic inventory regenerated with the tool because the new helper is tracked source (2202 -> 2203).

Matrix moves for the first time in this run: PASS 126 -> 127, FAIL 93 -> 92, NOT_APPLICABLE 88, NOT_ASSESSED 38. One control closed, honestly, with its two remaining boundaries named: Clear-Site-Data is honoured only in a secure context, and this covers explicit logout rather than idle session expiry.

The coverage registry is in scope because this pass adds a spec to the executed list, so its executedCount/discoveredCount describe this change: 21/915. The autopilot guard caught the omission before merge - the file had been edited without being declared - which is the scope gate doing exactly its job.
